metadata.title: USING A MACHINE LEARNING APPROACH TO EXPLORE NON-COGNITIVE FACTORS AFFECTING READING, MATHEMATICS, AND SCIENCE LITERACY IN CHINA AND THE UNITED STATES

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for two country samples (China and the United States) and applies a CART decision-tree model to classify students into low vs high ability groups and to identify top predictors. The manuscript states that PISA uses a stratified sample approach, but it does not report whether complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate weights were applied in the CART training or evaluation. Because CART is implemented as a standard supervised learning algorithm and the paper does not describe weight-aware training, it is unclear whether the analysis is population-representative at the student level. The preprocessing described includes setting missing values to 0, deleting cases with more than half missingness, and then applying k-nearest-neighbor interpolation, after which PV1READ/PV1MATH/PV1SCIE are used as dependent variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the OECD PISA 2018 database restricted to Chinese students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang provinces/cities and to United States students. The analysis combines student questionnaires including ICT familiarity and social background questionnaires. After deleting invalid questionnaires, the final analytic sample is 11,977 in China and 4,838 in the United States. For missing data, the study sets missing values of variables to 0, deletes samples with more than half missing values, and then uses k-nearest neighbor interpolation; after this, 62 variables are used for China and 73 variables are used for the United States (with ICT questionnaire differences handled by using only one ICT variable for China and nine ICT-related variables for the United States).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (PV1READ), age 15, China and United States
main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement (PV1READ) classified as low vs high
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (CART used; no accuracy/AUC/RMSE reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (PV1READ) data for age-15 students in China and the United States, the study leveraged meta-cognition assess credibility (METASPAM), meta-cognition summarizing (METASUM), understanding and remembering (UNDREM), enjoyment of reading (JOYREAD), and perceived PISA test difficulty (PISADIFF) to classify reading achievement into low vs high groups, finding that these non-cognitive factors were among the most influential predictors (with METASPAM ranked highest in China and PISADIFF ranked highest in the United States). This indicates that strengthening students’ metacognitive strategies and reading motivation—while also addressing how students perceive test difficulty—may improve reading performance, though the paper does not report predictive accuracy and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Mathematics (PV1MATH), age 15, China and United States
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (PV1MATH) classified as low vs high
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (CART used; no accuracy/AUC/RMSE reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics (PV1MATH) data for age-15 students in China and the United States, the study leveraged meta-cognition assess credibility (METASPAM), meta-cognition summarizing (METASUM), socioeconomic status (ESCS/WEALTH depending on country), science learning time (SMINS), and school lessons per week (ST060Q01NA) to classify mathematics achievement into low vs high groups, finding that student-level metacognitive variables were central in both countries while family socioeconomic indicators differed in prominence. This indicates that mathematics improvement efforts should prioritize metacognitive development and learning-time/lesson-structure supports, and also target students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, though the study’s CART performance metrics and causal identification are not provided.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Science (PV1SCIE), age 15, China and United States
main_findings.target_variable: Science achievement (PV1SCIE) classified as low vs high
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (CART used; no accuracy/AUC/RMSE reported).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science (PV1SCIE) data for age-15 students in China and the United States, the study leveraged meta-cognition assess credibility (METASPAM), meta-cognition summarizing (METASUM), science learning time (SMINS), school lessons per week (ST060Q01NA), and sense of belonging (BELONG) to classify science achievement into low vs high groups, finding that student-level metacognition and school-level learning-time variables were among the most influential predictors. This indicates that science interventions may benefit from combining metacognitive strategy instruction with increased and well-structured science learning opportunities, while also fostering students’ school belonging, though the paper does not report model fit metrics and cannot infer causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 microdata for age-15 students in China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang; N=11,977) and the United States (N=4,838) to explore how non-cognitive factors relate to reading, mathematics, and science literacy. Dependent variables are PV1READ, PV1MATH, and PV1SCIE, which are dichotomized into low vs high ability using achievement-level thresholds, and CART decision trees are trained separately by subject and country to identify the most influential predictors. The paper reports that the top common predictors include metacognition (METASPAM, METASUM), perceived PISA test difficulty (PISADIFF), and, at the school level, science learning time (SMINS) and weekly lesson counts (ST060Q01NA), with family socioeconomic indicators (ESCS in China; WEALTH in the United States) also important. However, no CART predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) are reported, and the manuscript does not document whether survey weights were used. Missing data handling is described (set to 0, delete >50% missing, then kNN interpolation), but the approach may affect stability if not applied within cross-validation folds.
